indicator.subject: Science
indicator.content_standard: B1.1.2.2: Know that substances can exist in different physical state (Solid, Liquid, Gas). Many substances can be changed from one state to another by heating or cooling
indicator.objective: Identify and classify materials as solid, liquid or gas

skills.description: Identify whether a named material is a solid, liquid or gas
Sort a small set of materials into solid, liquid and gas groups
Give an example of a solid, a liquid and a gas
Give a simple reason why a material belongs to a given state

misconceptions: Air is nothing, so it is not a gas.
Sand is a liquid because it pours.
Steam is not a gas because we can see it.
A solid cannot change shape at all.

questions.stem: Which of these is a solid?
hints: You can hold it in your hand.
questions.explanation: A stone is a solid. It has a fixed shape.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think any object is a solid, including liquids in a cup.

questions.stem: Which of these is a liquid?
questions.explanation: Water is a liquid. It flows and takes the shape of its container.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think water is the only liquid.

questions.stem: What state of matter is the air we breathe?
questions.explanation: Air is a gas. It fills the space around us.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think air is nothing, not a gas.

questions.stem: Which of these is a gas?
questions.explanation: Steam is a gas. It is water in its gaseous state.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think steam is liquid water.

questions.stem: Why is a table called a solid?
hints: Can you change its shape easily?
questions.explanation: A table is a solid because it has a fixed shape and does not flow.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think solids must be heavy.

questions.stem: Which group has only liquids?
questions.explanation: Water, milk, and juice are all liquids.
questions.misconception: Pupils may include stones in the liquids group if they think of pouring them.

questions.stem: Is a balloon filled with air a solid, liquid, or gas?
questions.explanation: The air inside the balloon is a gas.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the balloon itself is the gas because it is round.

questions.stem: Why is water called a liquid?
options: It takes the shape of its container
hints: Does it take the shape of the cup?
questions.explanation: Water is a liquid because it flows and takes the shape of whatever container it is in.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think water is liquid because it is wet, not because of its shape.

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT a solid?
questions.explanation: Milk is a liquid. You can pour it. The others are solids.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think anything white is a solid (like chalk).

questions.stem: Which of these is an example of a solid?
questions.explanation: Wood is a solid. It has a fixed shape.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think only hard things are solids.

questions.stem: What state of matter is ice?
questions.explanation: Ice is a solid. It is frozen water.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think ice is a liquid because it melts.

questions.stem: Give one example of a gas.
hints: What comes from a boiling pot?
questions.explanation: Air, steam, and smoke are examples of gases.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think gas is only petrol.

questions.stem: Ama has three items: a piece of chalk, a glass of water, and a balloon full of air. What are their states?
questions.explanation: Chalk is a solid, water is a liquid, and air is a gas.
questions.misconception: Pupils may get confused by the balloon, thinking the balloon is the gas.

questions.stem: Why does a gas not have a fixed shape?
options: It fills any container it is in
hints: Think about the air in a tyre.
questions.explanation: A gas spreads out to fill any container it is put into, so it does not have a fixed shape.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think gas has no shape because they cannot see it.

questions.stem: Which statement is TRUE?
options: Liquids take the shape of their container
Solids do not take up space
hints: Think about water in a cup.
questions.explanation: Liquids take the shape of their container. Solids keep their shape, and gases fill their container.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think liquids keep their shape like solids.

questions.stem: Kwesi blows into a balloon. What state of matter fills the balloon?
hints: What comes out of his mouth?
questions.explanation: The air Kwesi blows into the balloon is a gas.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the balloon is filled with liquid because it can burst.

questions.stem: Why is a stone a solid?
questions.explanation: A stone is a solid because it has a fixed shape and does not flow.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think stones are solids because they are heavy.

questions.stem: Explain why a liquid is different from a solid.

criteria.description: States that liquids take the shape of their container (while solids keep their shape)

hints: What happens when you pour water?
questions.explanation: Liquids flow and take the shape of their container, while solids keep their own shape.

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT true about gases?
options: They fill the space they are in
They can be compressed into a smaller space
hints: Think about the air in a tyre.
questions.explanation: Gases do not have a fixed shape; they spread out to fill their container.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think gases have a shape because they are inside objects.

questions.stem: Look around your classroom. Write down one solid and one liquid you can see.

criteria.description: Names a correct solid from the classroom
Names a correct liquid from the classroom (e.g., water in a bottle)

questions.explanation: Desks are solids, and water in a bottle is a liquid.
